Title: Chapter 13 -multi-scale modeling of tissues using compucell3d
Abstract: The study of how cells interact to produce tissue development, homeostasis, or diseases was, until recently, almost purely experimental. Now, multi-cell computer simulation methods, ranging from relatively simple cellular automata to complex immersed-boundary and finite-element mechanistic models, allow in silico study of multi-cell phenomena at the tissue scale based on biologically observed cell behaviors and interactions such as movement, adhesion, growth, death, mitosis, secretion of chemicals, chemotaxis, etc. This tutorial introduces the lattice-based Glazier–Graner–Hogeweg (GGH) Monte Carlo multi-cell modeling and the open-source GGH-based CompuCell3D simulation environment that allows rapid and intuitive modeling and simulation of cellular and multi-cellular behaviors in the context of tissue formation and subsequent dynamics. We also present a walkthrough of four biological models and their associated simulations that demonstrate the capabilities of the GGH and CompuCell3D.

gold.abstract: Mechanistic, multicellular, agent-based models are commonly used to investigate tissue, organ, and organism-scale biology at single-cell resolution. The Cellular-Potts Model (CPM) is a powerful and popular framework for developing and interrogating these models. CPMs become computationally expensive at large space- and time- scales making application and investigation of developed models difficult. Surrogate models may allow for the accelerated evaluation of CPMs of complex biological systems. However, the stochastic nature of these models means each set of parameters may give rise to different model configurations, complicating surrogate model development. In this work, we leverage denoising diffusion probabilistic models to train a generative AI surrogate of a CPM used to investigate in vitro vasculogenesis. We describe the use of an image classifier to learn the characteristics that define unique areas of a 2-dimensional parameter space. We then apply this classifier to aid in surrogate model selection and verification. Our CPM model surrogate generates model configurations 20,000 timesteps ahead of a reference configuration and demonstrates approximately a 22x reduction in computational time as compared to native code execution. Our work represents a step towards the implementation of DDPMs to develop digital twins of stochastic biological systems.

gold.title: Generative diffusion model surrogates for mechanistic agent-based biological models

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b contributes the Glazier–Graner–Hogeweg (GGH) multi-cell modeling framework and CompuCell3D, which simulate tissue-scale cell behaviors—movement, adhesion, growth, death, mitosis, secretion, chemotaxis—based on local cell interactions and extracellular fields.
- Paper-c contributes a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) approach that directly generates steady-state heat conduction and incompressible fluid flow fields from boundary/domain observations, without iterative numerical solution of the governing equations.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use the cGAN as a learned surrogate for extracellular transport fields inside CompuCell3D. In each GGH simulation step, the current cell configuration defines a domain and boundary conditions; the cGAN predicts the resulting nutrient, oxygen, or morphogen field. That field then feeds back into cell behaviors such as growth, chemotaxis, or differentiation. This causally links CompuCell3D’s tissue geometry generation to paper-c’s field inference, replacing or accelerating numerical reaction-diffusion/flow solvers.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Generate many 2D tissue domains with varying cell adhesion, growth, and boundary conditions in CompuCell3D. Compute corresponding transport fields using CompuCell3D’s standard diffusion solver as training data. Train a cGAN on tissue-domain masks plus boundary conditions to predict the field. Validate field accuracy with mean absolute error against the solver. Then couple the cGAN back into GGH updates and compare tissue-level outcomes—cell sorting, growth rate, pattern formation—and computation time against full PDE-coupled simulations. Missing cross-paper knowledge: exact CompuCell3D field-solver data formats and cGAN hyperparameters for irregular multicellular domains are not specified in either paper.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose a hybrid tissue-simulation framework that embeds a cGAN transport-field surrogate within CompuCell3D. Cellular configurations from GGH simulations generate domain geometry and boundary conditions; the cGAN directly predicts extracellular transport fields, which drive cell behavior. Validation compares field accuracy, tissue morphology, and speed against standard PDE-coupled CompuCell3D runs.

FINAL IDEA: A cGAN transport surrogate trained on CompuCell3D tissue domains can replace iterative reaction-diffusion solvers to accelerate and enhance multi-scale tissue simulations.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: CompuCell3D/GGH multi-cell modeling simulates cell movement, adhesion, growth, death, mitosis, secretion, and chemotaxis, generating tissue-scale cell configurations and associated chemical fields.
- Paper-c: A conditional GAN (cGAN) learns to directly generate steady-state heat conduction and incompressible fluid flow solutions from arbitrary boundary conditions and domain geometry, without governing equations, with high test accuracy.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
CompuCell3D produces time-varying cell-derived source/sink maps and moving tissue boundary conditions. A cGAN is trained on these CC3D outputs to act as a learned surrogate for tissue transport field updates: given a cell configuration, it predicts the steady-state chemical field that CC3D would otherwise compute. This is an operational coupling: CC3D supplies realistic biological input–output pairs; cGAN supplies fast, equation-free field inference.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Generate paired training data by running a CC3D monolayer model with a secreted diffusible morphogen, degradation, and fixed/absorbing boundaries; save cell-density/source maps, boundary masks, and CC3D-computed steady-state concentration fields. Train the cGAN to map source+boundary to concentration. Validate on held-out CC3D cases using MAE, gradient error, and structural similarity. Then couple the surrogate into CC3D, replacing field updates with cGAN predictions, and compare chemotactic cell patterns and runtimes against native CC3D simulations. Missing cross-paper knowledge: source papers do not report CC3D field-solver implementation cost or cGAN performance on spatially varying biological source fields.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project replaces iterative tissue-scale transport solving in CompuCell3D with a conditional GAN surrogate trained on CC3D-generated chemical fields. We test whether the cGAN can predict steady-state morphogen distributions from dynamic cell-source maps and boundary masks, and whether coupled cGAN-CC3D simulations reproduce chemotaxis-driven tissue patterns faster than native field computation. The contribution is a data-driven transport module embedded in an established multi-cell modeling framework, enabling rapid tissue simulation without governing equations.

FINAL IDEA: Use CompuCell3D-generated cell-source and chemical-field pairs to train a conditional GAN as a fast surrogate transport solver for chemotaxis-driven tissue simulations.

In coupled GGH runs, every 50 Monte Carlo steps the cGAN predicts the updated steady-state field from the fixed cell configuration; that field drives chemotaxis for the next block. We propose a quasi-steady cGAN transport surrogate inside CompuCell3D.
